# Embedded skill: ui-design-critique

# UI Design Critique (Apple HIG + UX Writing)

Critique interface screenshots and mockups the way a rigorous Apple design reviewer would: short, specific, honest, and grounded in named principles rather than vague opinion. Every observation ties to a principle the reader can look up.

Default to a **short critique they can scan**. Long-form prose is a failure. Depth is opt-in.

The bar: a designer should learn *why* something is weak in one line, not after a paragraph. Praise must be as specific as the criticism — never generic ("looks clean!") filler.

## When to run

Run this skill whenever a UI image is shared and any judgment is invited — including implicit invitations. "Here's the new pricing page" is an invitation. So is a bare screenshot with no text. Assume feedback is wanted unless the user says otherwise.

Do NOT run when:
- The image isn't an interface (a photo, chart, logo in isolation, illustration).
- The user explicitly asks only to implement/build/code with no review.
- The user asks a narrow factual question about the image ("what font is this?") — answer that directly instead.

## Before you critique — pick a mode

- **Short mode (default).** Score + working / not working bullets + one Fix first. No jargon. No section dump. This is the answer for a bare screenshot, "review this", "critique this", or any share without an explicit ask for depth.
- **Deep mode.** Only when they ask for a full breakdown, "deep", "all sections", or "go further". Short critique first, then the section list. Each section is 2–4 one-sentence bullets, never paragraphs.

If they already said they want depth, skip Short-as-final and go Deep after the Quick read.

## Step 1 — Read the screen before judging it

Before writing anything, study the image carefully and establish:

1. **Platform.** Desktop/web or mobile? Look at proportions, control sizes, chrome (menu bars, window controls, browser UI), and density. State it. If ambiguous, say so and critique for the most likely one. Most work here is **desktop/web** — default there when unsure.
2. **Purpose.** What is this screen *for*? What is the single most important thing a user should be able to do or understand here? (Apple: every screen has one purpose.) You will judge everything against this.
3. **Context.** Marketing page, product UI, settings, onboarding, empty/error state, form, dashboard? The conventions differ.

Do not skip this. Put it on **one line** under the Quick read (`Platform · Purpose · Context`). A critique that misreads purpose is worse than no critique.

## Step 2 — Write the short critique (always)

This is the default deliverable. Hard cap: **120 words**. Prefer 6–10 bullets. Never a 3–5 sentence overview paragraph.

```
## Quick read

**Score: X/10** — one sentence: what the screen is, whether it works, the headline issue.

Platform · Purpose · Context

**Working**
- one or two short bullets

**Not working**
- 2–4 short bullets: issue, then the fix, same line

**Fix first** — the single most important change, one line.
```

**Score:** out of 10, anchored to principles, not taste. 10 honors clarity, deference, consistency, accessibility, and PACE across the board. 5 has real structural issues but isn't broken. Below 4 means the screen doesn't communicate its purpose or has systemic failures. Be honest — inflating scores destroys trust.

No law names in the Quick read. Everyday language.

If this is Short mode, stop here plus one follow-up line: "Want the full breakdown?"

## Step 3 — Deep mode only (when asked)

Use this exact section order. **2–4 one-sentence bullets per section**, not prose. Length does not scale into essays — a dense dashboard gets more *points*, not more paragraphs.

```
## First impression & clarity of purpose
## Layout, hierarchy & spacing
## Typography
## Color & contrast (incl. accessibility)
## Components & interaction patterns
## Copywriting
## Psychology (cognitive load, affordance, trust, friction)
## Desktop/web vs mobile
## Verdict — fix these first
```

**Every point must name a principle** in the same bullet (e.g. "clarity", "deference", "Gestalt proximity", "Purpose/PACE", "Fitts's law", "consistency"). If you can't name the principle, drop the point.

### First impression & clarity of purpose
The 3-second read. Does the purpose (Step 1) announce itself, or does the eye wander? Apple's first principle is **clarity**. Name what the eye lands on first and whether that matches purpose.

### Layout, hierarchy & spacing
Visual hierarchy, alignment, spacing rhythm. Ground in **Gestalt** (proximity, similarity, common region, continuity, closure) and **deference**. Flag inconsistent spacing, weak grid, cramped targets. See `references/apple-design.md`.

### Typography
Limited type scale vs muddle; legibility (size, line length ~45–75 chars, line height, contrast). Ground in **clarity** and **aesthetic integrity**.

### Color & contrast (incl. accessibility)
Palette discipline, semantic color, WCAG (4.5:1 body, 3:1 large text ≥24px or ≥19px bold). Warn when color alone carries meaning. Flag low-contrast gray-on-white secondary text.

### Components & interaction patterns
**Consistency** and **affordance**. Flag reinvented controls with no benefit, and destructive actions without safeguards.

### Copywriting
Labels, buttons, headings, errors, empty states through **PACE**. Buttons are verb phrases naming the outcome. Quote the exact weak string and rewrite it on the same bullet. See `references/apple-copywriting.md`.

### Psychology
Hick's law, Miller's ~7±2, affordance/signifiers, trust, friction. Name the effect in the bullet.

### Desktop/web vs mobile
One or two bullets: what breaks on the other platform. Pointer vs touch (**Fitts's law**, ~44×44pt touch). Don't hide critical affordances behind hover.

### Verdict — fix these first
Prioritized numbered list. Highest-leverage first (clarity / accessibility / trust before polish). Each item: the fix, the principle, one line on impact. End with the single most important change if they only do one thing.

## After the critique

One line. Short mode: "Want the full breakdown?" Deep mode: "Did I read the purpose right?"

## Tone

Short, well-formed, specific, honest. Bullets, not essays. No hedging, no padding, no generic praise. When something is good, name the principle in the same bullet. When something is weak, put the fix in the same bullet.

## References

Load these for depth when a section needs it — they carry the detailed vocabulary and before/after examples:

- `references/apple-design.md` — Apple's design principles (Clarity, Deference, Depth), the classic macOS HIG heuristics, Gestalt principles, spacing/hierarchy/type/contrast checklists, and Fitts's/Hick's/Miller's laws.
- `references/apple-copywriting.md` — Apple's PACE framework (Purpose, Anticipation, Context, Empathy), voice-vs-tone, and a component-by-component copy pattern library (buttons, labels, placeholders, errors, empty states, confirmations, destructive actions, tooltips, changelogs, loading) with before/after pairs.

Primary sources these distill (point the user here to go deeper):
- Apple HIG: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines and .../design-principles
- WWDC "Writing for interfaces" (2022, 2024, 2025), "Designing Fluid Interfaces" (2018)
- Rene Wang, "Wording in Interfaces": https://rene.wang/essay/wording-in-interfaces

# Embedded reference: Apple design principles

# Apple Design Principles & Critique Vocabulary

Use this to ground the layout, typography, color, components, and psychology sections in named principles. Cite the principle by name in the critique.

## Apple's three core themes (modern HIG)

- **Clarity.** Text is legible at every size, icons are precise, adornments are subtle, and the design sharpens focus on function. Negative space, color, fonts, and imagery all work to highlight what matters. *Failure looks like:* nothing dominates, decoration competing with content, ambiguous icons.
- **Deference.** The UI helps people understand and interact with content but never competes with it. Chrome (bars, controls, backgrounds) recedes; content leads. *Failure looks like:* heavy borders/shadows/gradients pulling attention off the actual content, a loud shell around quiet substance.
- **Depth.** Visual layers and realistic motion convey hierarchy and give life; transitions communicate where you are and where you came from. *Failure looks like:* flat, ambiguous stacking; state changes with no motion cue.

## Classic macOS HIG heuristics (still cited)

These predate the three themes and remain useful vocabulary:

- **Metaphors** — familiar real-world concepts lower learning cost.
- **Direct manipulation** — users act on visible objects and see immediate results.
- **See-and-point (recognition over recall)** — show options rather than requiring memorized commands.
- **Feedback** — every action produces a visible, immediate response.
- **Consistency** — same thing looks/behaves the same everywhere, within the app and with platform conventions.
- **WYSIWYG** — what you see is what you get; no hidden state.
- **User control** — the user initiates and controls actions, not the app.
- **Forgiveness** — actions are reversible; destructive ones are guarded; errors are recoverable.
- **Perceived stability** — a consistent, understandable structure the user can rely on.
- **Aesthetic integrity** — the look matches the function and the content's seriousness.
- **Modelessness** — avoid trapping the user in modes that change what the same action does.
- **Accessibility** — usable by the widest range of people and abilities.

## Gestalt principles (for layout & hierarchy)

How the eye groups elements. Name the specific one:

- **Proximity** — things placed close together are read as related. Misuse: even spacing everywhere, so nothing groups; or a label far from its field.
- **Similarity** — shared color/shape/size implies same category. Misuse: unrelated items styled alike; related items styled differently.
- **Common region** — a shared background/border groups items. Cards, panels.
- **Continuity** — the eye follows lines and alignment; strong edges guide reading order.
- **Closure** — the mind completes shapes; lets you imply structure without heavy borders.
- **Figure/ground** — clear separation of foreground content from background. Weak figure/ground = content that doesn't pop.
- **Common fate** — elements moving together are grouped (motion/animation).

## Hierarchy & spacing checklist

- Is there ONE clear focal point per screen that matches the stated purpose? (Squint test: what survives when you blur the image?)
- Does hierarchy use multiple reinforcing signals (size + weight + color + position + whitespace), not just one?
- Is the spacing built on a consistent scale (e.g. 4/8pt system)? Random gaps read as sloppy; a rhythm reads as intentional.
- Is whitespace used to group (proximity) and to give the focal point room, or is everything crammed edge-to-edge (deference failure — no breathing room for content)?
- Is alignment disciplined? Elements should share edges/baselines on a grid. Stray misalignments read as errors even when users can't name them.
- Are related controls grouped and unrelated ones separated (proximity + common region)?

## Typography checklist

- **Scale:** a small, deliberate set of sizes/weights with clear jumps between levels. If body, caption, and subhead are within a couple points of each other, hierarchy collapses.
- **Legibility:** body text large enough (≥16px web body is a safe floor), line height ~1.4–1.6, line length ~45–75 characters. Too-long lines tire the eye; too-short lines fragment reading.
- **Pairing:** ideally one family, two at most, with roles (display vs text). More families fragment the voice (aesthetic-integrity / consistency).
- **Balance:** avoid widows/orphans in headlines and short blocks — rewrite or rebalance line breaks so paragraphs make even shapes. Users feel this as care.
- **Alignment:** left-aligned for long-form Latin text; avoid justified text on the web (uneven rivers). Centered text only for short blocks.

## Color & contrast checklist

- **Discipline:** a limited palette with defined roles (primary, neutral ramp, one or two accents, semantic success/warning/danger). A page with many unrelated hues reads as chaotic.
- **Semantic consistency:** if blue means "interactive" once, it must mean it everywhere; don't reuse the action color for decoration.
- **Contrast (WCAG 2):** body/normal text ≥ **4.5:1**; large text (≥24px, or ≥19px bold) ≥ **3:1**; UI components and graphical objects ≥ **3:1** against adjacent colors. The most common real-world failure is light-gray secondary text on white.
- **Never rely on color alone** to convey meaning (state, required fields, errors, chart series) — pair with text, icon, or shape. This is an explicit Apple accessibility rule and helps colorblind and low-vision users.
- **Dark mode / elevation:** if shown, check that layers are distinguishable and contrast holds.

## Interaction & cognitive laws

- **Fitts's law** — time to hit a target grows as it shrinks and as it gets farther away. Implication: important/frequent controls should be larger and closer; touch targets ≥ ~44×44pt; screen corners/edges are "infinite" targets (easy to hit). Pointer input tolerates smaller, denser targets than touch.
- **Hick's law** — decision time grows with the number/complexity of choices. Implication: reduce or group options; use progressive disclosure; don't present ten equal-weight actions.
- **Miller's law (~7±2)** — working memory is limited; chunk information into groups.
- **Jakob's law** — users expect your product to work like the others they already know; deviating from platform conventions costs them effort (ties to consistency).
- **Affordances & signifiers** — an affordance is a possible action; a signifier is the perceptible cue that reveals it (a button that looks raised/tappable). Flat design often strips signifiers — check that interactive elements still *look* interactive and static ones don't.
- **Aesthetic-usability effect** — attractive interfaces are perceived as more usable and are more forgiven for minor issues; polish buys goodwill but never substitutes for clarity.

## Motion (when relevant / from "Designing Fluid Interfaces")

- Motion should be **interruptible, responsive, and continuous** — tied to user input, not canned animations that block interaction.
- Transitions should communicate spatial relationships (where this came from, where it goes) — supporting **depth**.
- Gratuitous animation that delays the user violates deference and user control.

# Embedded reference: Apple copywriting

# Apple UX Writing & Interface Copy Patterns

Use this to ground the Copywriting section. Every word in an interface is a design decision; strip away the visuals and the text does most of the work. A pixel-perfect layout with lazy copy reads as broken — the gap is trust. Quote the actual strings from the screenshot and rewrite the weak ones.

## PACE framework (Apple, "Writing for interfaces")

The lens Apple's own UX writers use. PACE = keeping a natural flow so people stay oriented.

- **Purpose.** Every screen has one most-important thing to convey. Establish information hierarchy (headline states the purpose; buttons are clear on their own). Know what to leave out — cut, move, or demote secondary ideas. Tell people the purpose; it's not a secret. Aim for simplicity over exhaustive detail.
- **Anticipation.** Treat the interface as a conversation with back-and-forth. Anticipate the user's next question or action and answer it in place ("What comes next?"). Develop one **voice**, then vary **tone** by situation (celebratory for a milestone, calm and plain in a stressful moment). Use exclamation points rarely.
- **Context.** Consider what's happening outside the app (busy, driving, glancing) and write for that attention budget. Alerts are interruptions — make them helpful, name the specific action on the buttons (never bare Yes/No), put the destructive option clearly. Errors should say what went wrong and exactly what to do. Empty states educate or celebrate and always guide what goes here.
- **Empathy.** Write for everyone: simple, plain language; avoid idioms/humor that don't translate or exclude. Be localization-aware (text length varies, RTL exists). Write thoughtful, descriptive accessibility text for every element, symbol, and image — for some users that text *is* the interface. Prefer "person" over gendered nouns.

Final Apple tip: **read the copy out loud** — it exposes stiffness, repetition, and errors, and checks that it sounds like talking to a friend.

## Voice vs tone

- **Voice** is constant (who the product is — playful game vs trustworthy bank vs kid-friendly app). Define what it would and wouldn't say; keep a term list.
- **Tone** flexes with the moment. Same voice, different tone for an error vs a celebration.

## Component-level copy patterns (before → after)

Cite these when critiquing specific strings. The principle is in **bold**.

- **Buttons — name the outcome (verb phrase).** "Help" (a noun/category) → "Get Help". "Desktop App" → "Download Desktop App". A button label is a promise of what clicking does.
- **Buttons in flows — name the destination.** "Next" → "Continue to payment". Naming where you're going removes a blind-trust click.
- **Settings labels — describe the experience, not the tech.** "Enable two-factor authentication" → "Require a code to sign in". Give toggles a clear on-state ("Send me email notifications"). Use **positive phrasing**: "Renew automatically" beats "Disable auto-renewal". Name the real category ("Billing", not "Advanced"). Descriptions should add new info, not repeat the title.
- **Placeholder text — describe scope, not mechanics.** "Enter keywords" → "Search issues, projects, pages". For inputs, show an example ("contact@rene.wang") rather than restating the field.
- **Error messages — problem + reason + path forward.** "Invalid input." → "This email is already registered. Try signing in instead." Avoid "oops/uh-oh" (patronizing) and hollow "sorry/please".
- **Confirmations — echo the action and the object.** "Successfully saved." → "Your changes to 'Project Alpha' have been saved." Vague reassurance is noise.
- **Empty states — echo intent + offer a next step.** "No results found." → "No results for 'fluxcap'. Try a different keyword or check your spelling." The highest-leverage overlooked moment.
- **Destructive actions — list consequences, don't escalate fear.** Not "WARNING… permanent… irreversible… cannot be undone" (three synonyms, no information) → "Delete 'Landing Page'? 12 published posts will be unpublished · 3 team members will lose access · Cannot be undone." Reframe the safe button as a positive choice ("Keep project" beats "Cancel"). Consequences inform; fear becomes noise users click through.
- **Disabled/locked states — name the reward, not just the gate.** "Available on Pro plan" → "Unlock custom domains → Pro". A disabled control is a desire signal; convert it.
- **Changelogs — describe the outcome, not the diff.** "Fixed custom font rendering issue" → "Your exports now include custom fonts." Name the specific fixed problem ("blank pages on Firefox", not "PDF bug"). Users care about their workflow, not your bugs.
- **Loading copy — name the action + set expectation.** "Please wait…" → "Generating your report (about 6 seconds)" with a live counter, so the wait feels intentional, not broken.
- **FAQ / answer length — brevity signals confidence.** For a trust-sensitive question ("Can I cancel anytime?"), "Yes. No fees, no questions." beats three qualified paragraphs. Length itself is a message; over-explaining reads as hiding.

## Cross-cutting copy rules

- **Consistency of terms.** Pick one noun and one verb per concept and hold them everywhere. "Remove member" for every row beats a mix of "Remove / Kick out / Delete user" — synonyms create micro-doubt ("is Kick out the same as Remove?"). Consistency is a contract that lets users stop reading carefully.
- **No relative dates in persistent copy.** "Expires in 72 hours" → "Expires March 27, 2026." Don't make the reader do math.
- **Positive over negative** phrasing for toggles and actions.
- **Specific over generic** everywhere — echo the user's object/query/action back to them.
- **Visual shape of text** matters: rewrite to kill widows and make paragraphs even; it reads as care.
- **Sentence case** for most Apple UI text (buttons, labels, titles) unless a strong reason for title case; be consistent either way.
